title: Indigenous rainforest peoples: the Yanomami

accuracy.evidence: Every figure checked against Survival International's Yanomami page (fetched Nov 23, 2026): about 45,000 people in northern Brazil and southern Venezuela; round shared yanos or shabonos for up to 400 people with an open central area; around 60 crops giving about 80% of food; hunting only about 10%; nuts, shellfish, larvae and 15 kinds of wild honey gathered; peccary, tapir, deer and monkey hunted; no hunter eats his own kill; a new garden every two or three years because Amazon soil is not very fertile; about 500 plants for food, medicine and building. Baka (Congo Basin) and Penan (Borneo) placed per Survival International. 'More than 10,000 years' in the Amazon follows Roosevelt et al. 1996 (Caverna da Pedra Pintada). Equal sharing in the lab is framed as fair sharing between families, which matches the documented sharing norm without claiming an exact rule.

misconceptions.evidence: Predictions and challenge target documented slips: forest homes from shop materials (predict 1, 'shop'), rainforest peoples live only by hunting (predict 2, 'hunt'; the 10% vs 80% figures), farming means clearing the whole forest (predict 3, 'cut'), indigenous peoples belong only to the past (predict 4, 'past'), all rainforest peoples are one group ('one'), and the hunter keeping his catch ('keep').

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built around this topic's own mechanisms: an ordered build of a round shared house (poles, then vines, then palm-leaf roof with an open centre), a 3-way grow / gather / hunt-or-fish sort, a 9-year shifting-garden simulation where tired soil forces a new small garden and the old patch regrows after 3 years, a rainforest-peoples-of-today placement across three rainforests with the equator, and sharing a hunter's catch with a 'keep it for the hunter' trap. None of these could be reused by relabelling.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by acting: wrong-order or factory parts are refused with a reason; foods only land in their true source; the garden stops giving food until a new patch is chosen and the old one visibly turns from tired soil to growing back to forest; the hunter's own pile is refused. The DONE text then confirms the idea and the prediction reveal.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'From a shop in a city' (factory cards are refused), 'Yes, mostly hunting' (garden foods outnumber hunted ones in the sort and the adult text gives 80% vs 10%), 'Cut down all the forest' (one small garden at a time; extra clearing is refused), 'No, only long ago' (three peoples placed on rainforests today).

challenge_feedback.evidence: slip() gives a specific message for each wrong tag: shop (house and food come from the forest), hunt (hunting is a small part; gardens give most), cut (one small new garden, old one regrows), past (they live there today), one (many peoples: Yanomami, Baka, Penan), keep (a hunter shares his catch).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words with a pronunciation guide for Yanomami; validate_lessons readability limits pass (kid within 6.5, adult within 9.5). Lab strips and buttons are 2 to 8 words.

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence teaches a fact or checks one; no filler phrases; the adult text gives curriculum links, figures with sources, wider context and common mistakes without repetition.

mobile.evidence: At 390 px the canvas uses the tall 1.3 ratio; the build cards wrap to 3 columns, the six garden patches to a 3 by 2 grid, the three bins and rainforests stay side by side with wrapped labels, and the young class gives large buttons below the canvas. Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark in the browser gate.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button (each house part, each bin per food, Next year and a button per forest patch, each rainforest, each family and 'Keep it for the hunter'). tell() updates the canvas aria-label and the polite live region after every action; the browser gate's axe run (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone.

sources: Roosevelt, A. C. et al. (1996), Paleoindian cave dwellers in the Amazon: the peopling of the Americas, Science 272(5260)
Kopenawa, D. and Albert, B. (2013), The Falling Sky: Words of a Yanomami Shaman, Harvard University Press
DfE (2013), National curriculum in England: geography KS1 (place knowledge, human and physical features, hot areas and the equator) and science KS1 (living things and their habitats)
